title: Hosted API shard imbalance + traffic surge retrospective
summary: On 2027-11-30 14:17 UTC the hosted API experienced a high-severity outage manifested as region-wide tail latency spikes and elevated 5xx rates for streaming sessions. Root cause was an unexpected traffic redistribution combined with shard placement imbalance in the streaming frontends that concentrated prefix-hot workloads on a subset of nodes. The overloaded frontends saturated KV-cache and connection-handling paths, producing cascading stream fragment errors and timed reconnects. Customer-facing impact: ~18 minutes of degraded streaming and increased error rate for long-running sessions across multiple customers; majority of non-stream (batch/generate) traffic unaffected.
timeline:
2027-11-30T14:10 UTC - small but rising prefix-hot traffic detected in our internal anomaly detector
2027-11-30T14:17 UTC - alert: hosted-api:streaming-tails-latency > 95th percentile threshold (pager triggered)
2027-11-30T14:18 UTC - SRE oncall acknowledged and triaged; initial hypothesis: KV cache hotspot or autoscaler lag
2027-11-30T14:20 UTC - graphing showed 6 frontends with 3-4x more active streaming sessions than neighbors; connection queue depth rising
2027-11-30T14:24 UTC - mitigation: soft-eviction of kv prefixes applied to overloaded frontends; routing policy temporarily adjusted to avoid those frontends
2027-11-30T14:30 UTC - partial recovery observed: streaming error-rate falling, tail-latency trending down but not at baseline
2027-11-30T14:35 UTC - roll-forward of a quick scheduler tweak to rebalance new sessions across shards; connection drain initiated on hot frontends
2027-11-30T14:45 UTC - normal streaming metrics restored; full verification and post-incident communication began
2027-11-30T15:05 UTC - incident declared resolved (service functional), follow-ups and RCA assigned
detection_and_alerting: Our anomaly detector first flagged prefix hotness at 14:10 UTC but the primary oncall notification came from the streaming tail-latency SLO pager at 14:17 UTC. Existing alerts were tuned to SLO thresholds, which caught the external customer impact quickly. However, we lacked a dedicated alert for frontend shard imbalance (skewed active session counts across shards) which would have pointed directly to the root cause earlier.
mitigations: Immediate steps: 1) Applied kv-prefix soft-eviction on the most overloaded frontends to relieve cache pressure and reduce tail latency; 2) Adjusted routing policy (in routing-control plane) to steer new sessions away from overloaded shards for short window; 3) Drained connections gracefully from the three hottest frontends to allow rebalance; 4) Increased streaming session acceptance window on adjacent shards to absorb incoming traffic. These mitigations gained symptom relief within ~10 minutes. We intentionally avoided a global autoscaler change because that would have increased churn and likely worsened prefix hotness.
root_cause: Traffic redistribution caused by several high-QPS customer workloads (spikes from a marketing launch) landed unevenly due to a recent scheduler tweak that changed the shard affinity heuristics. The scheduler change increased probability of assigning new streaming sessions to hot shards when the hotness metric was dominated by recent ephemeral session counts rather than smoothed load. This combined with insufficient KV cache eviction aggressiveness allowed hot prefixes to remain resident and force high KV cache miss latency and connection backpressure on those frontends.
contributing_factors:
- Recent scheduler affinity tweak deployed three days prior altered assignment randomness and reduced smoothing on active-session counts.
- No localized shard-skew alert existed; only aggregate SLO/latency alerts.
- KV cache eviction policy favored TTL over access-frequency, so prefix-hot workloads remained resident for longer than ideal.
- Our routing control plane did not have a low-latency way to retract shard assignments in-flight.
- Oncall had limited visibility into per-shard session counts in the default dashboard (needed a custom query)

SRE-2242: Add shard-skew alert (percentile-based difference in active sessions between shards) to catch imbalance early (owner: Priya Singh; due: 2027-12-06)
SRE-2243: Tweak KV cache eviction to weight recent access frequency higher for streaming prefixes (owner: Miguel Ramirez; due: 2027-12-14)
SRE-2244: Implement a routing-control quick-retract API to mark shards temporarily draining/avoid (owner: Lena Korhonen; due: 2028-01-10)

runbook_draft:
Purpose: provide an SRE playbook for shard-imbalance-driven streaming degradation.
Pre-req: ability to query per-shard session counts, kv-cache metrics, and trigger routing-control adjustments.
Immediate checks: 1) Check 'streaming-tail-latency' and 'streaming-5xx' SLO graphs; 2) Query per-shard active session counts and mark shards with >2x median; 3) Check kv-cache hit/miss and eviction rates for those shards; 4) Verify there was no upstream deploy to scheduler in last 72h (git/CI links).
Mitigation sequence: A) If per-shard skew > 2x: apply soft-eviction to hot prefixes on target shards (one shard at a time) and monitor latency for 60s; B) If soft-eviction insufficient: set routing-control flag to avoid hot shards for new sessions for 2-10 minutes and enable draining; C) If queue depth continues to climb: initiate graceful session drain on the single-most-hot shard and redistribute via scheduler; D) If global traffic surge persists: coordinate with product/customer teams to rate-limit offending client keys or request client backoff.
Post-mitigation: collect timeline, export heap/profile samples of frontend processes, and save kv-cache snapshots for the hot shards for offline analysis.
Escalation: if recovery not observed within 20 minutes, escalate to SRE lead and infra oncall (phone) and prepare for targeted rollback of scheduler-affinity change.
notes_to_oncall:
- When you see a streaming tail-latency pager, first check per-shard session distribution before assuming global capacity shortage.
- Soft-eviction is low-risk and should be tried early; it often gives quick wins for prefix-hot cases.
- Avoid full autoscaler triggers while diagnosing—adding nodes can increase distribution skew in the short term.
- Keep Slack incident channel summary crisp: include top-3 hot shard ids and current routing policy flags.
- This incident shows we need better pre-deploy gating for scheduler changes (add SRE-run load test to PR pipeline).
